title: Hadith commentary
hook: scholars like Ibn Hajar wrote vast commentaries

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forty tradition, and your line: forty to carry. How many sayings are in your pocket now? Say them in order. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

How much can be said about one sentence? Not a summary of it. An explanation. What each word means. Who carried it, and from whom. How another version words it. What scholars drew from it, and where they parted ways. Put all that under a line you could say in one breath, and it runs on for pages. The scholar Ibn Hajar wrote one of these on the whole of Sahih al-Bukhari, a vast work, saying by saying. That surrounding writing has a name. Today: sharh.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE.` → `EXPLAINED, NOT SUMMARIZED.` → `IBN HAJAR, SAYING BY SAYING.`

segments.voice: Sharh means explanation. It names a commentary written on a hadith collection, one report at a time. First, the writers. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani wrote Fath al-Bari, his commentary on Bukhari. Al-Nawawi, the compiler of yesterday's forty, wrote a commentary on Sahih Muslim. And the forties got commentaries of their own. Then, what a commentator actually does, with a line you already hold: actions are only by intentions. A commentator starts with the words. What is an intention, exactly? A passing thought, or a settled direction of the heart? Then the chain: who carried it, and from whom. Then the rest of the text, because the hadith doesn't stop where the slogan does. In its fuller versions in Bukhari it goes on: whoever emigrated for Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is for Allah and His Messenger, and whoever emigrated for something of this world, or to marry a woman, his emigration is for what he emigrated for. Read whole, the line is about the same outward act carrying two very different inner journeys. Then the questions of practice: does an act of worship count without an intention behind it? Here commentators lay out the views of earlier scholars, say who held them, and weigh them. Last, the posture of the whole genre. The saying sits in the center. The commentator stands around it, quoting others, disagreeing politely, admitting where he's unsure. The aim isn't to replace the Prophet's words but to keep them from being misread. Ibn Hajar also asks why al-Bukhari opened his book with this report, and one answer given is that the author was setting his own intention right before the work began.
screen: `SHARH: AN EXPLANATION.` · `FIRST THE WORDS, THEN THE CHAIN.` · `THE REST OF THE HADITH.` · `THE SAYING IN THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one commentary note, starting with your own. Settle, and breathe. Take the line: actions are only by intentions. Pick one word from it, just one. Actions, or only, or intentions. Hold it the way a commentator would. What does it mean? What would the line lose without it? Don't hurry to an answer. Then let the questions go, and rest with the whole line on the breath. Later today, if you can, find one real commentary note on this hadith and read it slowly. The bell holds the time.
Sharh. An explanation, a commentary written around a hadith collection, saying by saying, like Ibn Hajar's on Bukhari. Today's word.

Your line: explained for us. Today, when a short line of anything puzzles you, read what comes after it before deciding what it means. Tomorrow: reading hadith today. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Students of hadith read a collection alongside a commentary, such as Ibn Hajar's Fath al-Bari on Bukhari or al-Nawawi's commentary on Muslim, usually with a teacher who explains the commentary in turn.

fork.setup: you're writing a commentary. you reach a line whose meaning earlier scholars disagreed on. what do you write?
options: only the view you prefer, as if no other existed.

fork.reveal: commentaries lay out the earlier views, name who held them, and then weigh them. the disagreement stays on the page.

notes: Bukhari 1 opens the Sahih with the hadith on intentions; its first placement gives only the worldly half of the emigration clause. The fuller wording paraphrased here (whoever emigrated for Allah and His Messenger... / for something of this world or to marry a woman...) is cited to Bukhari 54 (also 6689). Confirm numbers and paraphrase.
Ibn Hajar discussing why al-Bukhari opened with this hadith, and the reading that it reflects the author's attention to his own intention: attributed as 'a reading people repeat'. Confirm.
'Commentaries lay out earlier views, name who held them, and weigh them' (fork reveal) is a general description of the genre; confirm.
'The forties got commentaries of their own' (e.g. Ibn Rajab's Jami' al-'Ulum wa al-Hikam on al-Nawawi's forty, not named here); confirm.
